overview.heading: Run the in-house lab so every result can be trusted
overview.intro: This lesson follows the supplied Laboratory Procedures course document exactly: four section bands — Hematology, Blood Chemistry, Urinalysis, and Additional Tests & Tips — each opening with its key terms, then the document's ten instructional modules of procedure detail, then a five-question final assessment at a 70% pass mark. Forty-six key terms are click-to-reveal cards, the reading panels keep the document's accordion pattern, and each procedure is reinforced with a short ordering, matching or classification activity.
objectives: Name the sample and tube each in-house test requires, including why EDTA samples need non-additive hematocrit tubes.
Prepare and evaluate a blood smear: controlled drop, pusher slide, feathered edge and monolayer, Diff-Quik staining, then 4x through 100x oil immersion.
Perform a packed cell volume and read total solids on the refractometer, noting plasma color and clarity.
Describe the Catalyst chemistry workflow and the SNAP test procedure, including conjugate lot matching and the control dot.
Run a urinalysis: dipstick, sediment analysis, and specific gravity on a refractometer rather than a dipstick pad.
Describe fecal flotation, fecal cytology and wet mounts, therapeutic drug monitoring timing, and ear cytology with the designated dirty stain.
overview.connectsForward: Sample Collection covers how each specimen reaches the lab; this lesson covers what happens to it once it arrives. Imaging Support and Case Presentation then cover the other half of the diagnostic picture and how findings are communicated. Five of the document's nine video locations are still placeholders, so each one carries a stable media key that lets a finished MP4 drop in without touching the surrounding lesson.

modules.content:
Hematology · Section 1 of 4

Hematology

The first of the document's four sections. Review the fifteen key terms used throughout the hematology material, then watch the section title video.

Before we get started, let's review a few key terms we'll go over in our first section…

0 of 15 key terms revealed

  • Hematology Analyzer

    A machine that analyzes blood samples to provide information about red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

  • EDTA

    Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, an anticoagulant added to blood collection tubes to prevent clotting. Purple top tubes typically contain EDTA.

  • Manual Differential

    A lab procedure where a technician examines a blood smear under a microscope to identify and count different types of white blood cells.

  • Cell Morphology

    The study of the size, shape, and structure of cells. Manual differentials are important for assessing cell morphology.

  • Blood Smear

    A thin layer of blood spread on a microscope slide used for microscopic examination.

  • Feathered Edge

    The thin, outer edge of a blood smear where cells are spread out in a single layer, ideal for examination.

  • Diff-Quick Stain

    A common staining technique using three solutions: a fixative (blue), an eosinophilic stain (pink), and a basophilic stain (purple).

  • Monolayer

    The area of a blood smear where cells are evenly distributed in a single layer, suitable for accurate cell counting and morphology assessment.

  • PCV (Packed Cell Volume)

    Also known as hematocrit, it measures the percentage of red blood cells in a volume of whole blood.

  • Total Solids (TS)

    Refers to the total protein concentration in blood plasma, commonly measured using a refractometer.

  • Heparinized Hematocrit Tubes

    Tubes pre-treated with heparin, another type of anticoagulant.

  • Buffy Coat

    The thin layer between the packed red blood cells and plasma in a centrifuged hematocrit tube. It contains white blood cells and platelets.

  • Non-Additive Hematocrit Tubes

    Tubes without any anticoagulant added, used when the blood sample already contains an anticoagulant.

  • Hemolysis

    The rupture or destruction of red blood cells, which can affect the color and clarity of blood plasma.

  • Refractometer

    An instrument used to measure the refractive index of a solution, correlated to the concentration of substances like protein in blood plasma.

modules.content:
Hematology · Instructional module 1 of 10

Hematology Analyzers & Manual Differentials

The first of the document's ten accordion modules. Open each section to read the source detail.

0 of 2 sections open

Automated hematology analyzers measure various parameters related to red blood cells and white blood cells. It is important to use whole blood collected in a purple top tube containing EDTA anticoagulant for these tests.

While hematology analyzers provide valuable information, they do not assess cell morphology. Manual differentials, where a veterinary technician examines a blood smear under a microscope, are necessary for evaluating the shape and appearance of cells.

Manual differentials can be more accurate, especially if the sample has clots, an insufficient volume, or an improper blood-to-anticoagulant ratio.

When the document says a manual differential can be more accurate

  • The sample has clots.
  • The sample volume is insufficient.
  • The blood-to-anticoagulant ratio is improper.

modules.content:
Hematology · Instructional module 2 of 10 · Document screen 2

Blood Smear Preparation

The document's second hematology screen. Read the source detail, watch the supplied demonstration video, then put the preparation steps in order.

0 of 4 sections open

Creating a blood smear allows for microscopic examination of individual blood cells, enabling assessment of cell morphology and the identification of different cell types (manual differential).

Use a whole blood sample collected in an EDTA tube. The sources describe various methods for placing a small drop of blood on a slide, including using a pipette, a cotton-tipped applicator, a wooden stick, or a microhematocrit tube. The microhematocrit tube is recommended as it helps control the sample size.

A 'pusher slide' is used to spread the blood drop across the slide in a smooth, even motion. The goal is to create a feathered edge, a thin area where cells are spread out in a single layer (monolayer), making them easier to view under a microscope.

Diff-Quik stain, a three-step process involving fixative (blue), eosinophilic stain (pink), and basophilic stain (purple), is commonly used to stain blood smears. The sources outline the dipping procedure and emphasize blotting excess stain between steps and rinsing the slide after staining.

Put the steps in order

Put the smear preparation and staining steps in the document's order

Select each step in the order the document describes. If a step comes later, the activity says so and nothing is lost.

0 of 7 steps in order

    Sequence complete. That is the document's order: EDTA sample, controlled drop, pusher slide, feathered edge, then the three Diff-Quik solutions with blotting between steps and a rinse at the end.

modules.content:
Hematology · Instructional module 3 of 10

Evaluating the Blood Smear

How the document says to work through a stained smear, and what it says to look for.

0 of 3 sections open

The sources recommend a systematic approach to examining the blood smear, starting at low magnification (4x) to scan for large abnormalities and assess the feathered edge. Evaluation continues at progressively higher magnifications (10x, 40x), culminating in the use of the oil immersion lens (100x) for detailed assessment of cell morphology and performing a manual differential.

When examining the blood smear, the veterinary technician looks for parasites, such as microfilaria (larval stage of heartworms), which might be visible in the feathered edge. Abnormally sized cells or cells with unusual shapes may be indicative of certain conditions. An excessive number of white blood cells pushed into the feathered edge could indicate the need for a new smear.

Platelet clumping can affect the accuracy of platelet counts. A manual differential involves counting different types of white blood cells (neutrophils, lymphocytes, etc.) and determining their percentages. This information helps in diagnosing various conditions. Changes in the shape or size of red blood cells can provide clues about underlying diseases.

Put the steps in order

Work up through the magnifications in the document's order

The document describes a systematic approach. Select each magnification in the order it is used.

0 of 4 steps in order

    Sequence complete. 4x, 10x, 40x, then 100x oil immersion for cell morphology and the manual differential.

modules.content:
Hematology · Instructional module 4 of 10 · Document screen 3

Packed Cell Volume (PCV) and Total Solids

The document's third hematology screen. This module includes the supplied Total Solids demonstration video.

0 of 3 sections open

PCV (or Hematocrit) measures the percentage of red blood cells in a whole blood sample. It is a crucial component of assessing anemia.

To perform a PCV, first select the appropriate type of hematocrit tube (heparinized or non-additive) based on the anticoagulant present in the blood sample. EDTA samples require non-additive tubes. Fill the tube about two-thirds full with well-mixed blood, seal the end of the tube with clay, balance the centrifuge with two tubes or a counterbalance, and centrifuge the sample at a designated speed and time (microhematocrit setting).

After centrifugation, the PCV is determined by measuring the height of the packed red blood cell layer against a graduated scale on a reading device or chart. In addition to the PCV, the color and clarity of the plasma are also noted, as these can provide valuable diagnostic information. For instance, hemolysis (breakdown of red blood cells) can cause the plasma to appear reddish.

Total Solids (Total Protein) measurement reflects the concentration of proteins in the plasma. It can be determined using a refractometer. The procedure involves breaking the hematocrit tube just above the buffy coat (the layer of white blood cells and platelets) to isolate the plasma, carefully placing a drop of plasma on the refractometer slide, and reading the total solids value from the refractometer scale.

Put the steps in order

Put the PCV steps in the document's order

Select each step in the order the document describes it.

0 of 6 steps in order

    Sequence complete. Select the tube, fill two-thirds, seal with clay, balance, spin on the microhematocrit setting, then read the packed cell column and note plasma color and clarity.

    Total solids follows the same tube

    The document describes breaking the hematocrit tube just above the buffy coat to isolate plasma, placing a drop of that plasma on the refractometer slide, and reading the total solids value from the scale.

    Measurement of chemical components in blood, providing information about organ health and function.

  • Catalyst Machine

    Automated blood chemistry analyzer used to perform blood tests.

  • Lithium Heparin Plasma

    Blood sample with lithium heparin anticoagulant, preferred for chemistry analysis.

    Specialized pipette for accurately measuring and dispensing specific liquid volumes.

  • Clips

    Coded clips in the Catalyst machine for identifying and initiating specific tests.

  • Reference Intervals

    Established normal ranges for blood chemistry tests; deviations may indicate abnormalities.

  • Glucose

    A sugar that is a major energy source; elevated levels can indicate diabetes.

modules.content:
Blood Chemistry · Instructional module 5 of 10

Chemistry Testing

The Catalyst analyzer workflow exactly as the document describes it.

0 of 3 sections open

The Catalyst analyzer discussed in the course is used to perform a variety of chemistry tests, including those assessing liver and kidney function, electrolytes, thyroid hormone levels, and more.

The procedure involves collecting the precise volume of plasma using a dedicated pipette for the Catalyst machine, transferring the plasma to a designated sample cup while minimizing the formation of bubbles, selecting the appropriate test clips for the desired panel (e.g., Chem 10 for a basic metabolic panel), and handling the clips carefully to avoid contaminating them with oils or debris.

Load the sample cup and clips into the Catalyst machine and initiate the test run. Results are typically available in 10-15 minutes. The Catalyst analyzer provides a printout or digital display of the test results along with their corresponding reference intervals. Abnormalities are often flagged or highlighted.

Put the steps in order

Put the Catalyst steps in the document's order

Select each step in the order the document describes it.

0 of 5 steps in order

    Sequence complete. Precise plasma with the dedicated pipette, transfer without bubbles, correct clips handled cleanly, then load, run and read against the reference intervals.

    What the document flags about the pipette and the clips

    • The pipette is dedicated to the Catalyst machine and collects a precise volume of plasma.
    • Bubbles are minimized when the plasma is transferred to the sample cup.
    • Clips are chosen for the ordered panel and handled carefully to avoid oils or debris.
    • Results are typically available in 10-15 minutes, with reference intervals and flagged abnormalities.

modules.content:
Blood Chemistry · Instructional module 6 of 10

SNAP Tests

Rapid in-house tests: which samples they accept, how the kit is used, and how results are read.

0 of 3 sections open

SNAP tests are rapid diagnostic tests used to detect a variety of conditions, including heartworm disease and tick-borne illnesses. SNAP tests can be performed using serum, EDTA plasma, lithium heparin plasma, or whole blood, depending on the specific test.

The test kit includes pipettes, tubes, and a conjugate. It's crucial to use the conjugate from the same box of tests as the lot numbers are tested together. A specific number of drops of the sample and conjugate are added to the tube and mixed. The entire contents of the tube are then poured into the sample well of the SNAP test. The test can be read manually or using a SNAP reader.

The SNAP reader displays an image of the test well, showing the control dot and any other dots that have developed, indicating a positive result. The test itself also shows the results, with dots appearing for positive findings.

modules.content:
Urinalysis · Section 3 of 4

Urinalysis

The document's third section. Review the twelve urinalysis key terms before the urinalysis procedures.

Before we get started, let's review a few key terms we'll go over in this upcoming section…

0 of 12 key terms revealed

  • Urine Dipstick

    A plastic strip with chemically treated pads that change color when dipped in urine, indicating various substances.

  • Urine Analyzer

    A device that automates urine dipstick readings, providing digital results and eliminating subjective visual comparisons.

  • Manual Urinalysis

    Performing urinalysis without an analyzer, requiring visual comparison of dipstick colors to a reference chart.

  • Urine Sediment Analyzer

    A machine that analyzes urine sediment, identifying components like white blood cells, red blood cells, and bacteria.

  • Stained vs. Unstained

    Microscopic examination of urine sediment using stains to enhance visibility, or observing in natural state without staining.

  • Wet Mount

    A technique where a drop of urine is placed on a slide, covered with a coverslip, and viewed under a microscope.

  • Dry Mount

    A technique where urine is spread and air-dried on a slide before staining and microscopic examination.

  • Urine Specific Gravity

    A measure of the concentration of dissolved substances in urine, indicating the kidney's ability to concentrate urine.

  • Cystocentesis

    A technique for collecting urine directly from the bladder using a needle and syringe.

  • Urine Color

    A visual assessment of urine color, ranging from pale yellow to dark amber, depending on hydration and substances.

  • Urine Clarity

    A visual assessment of urine transparency, described as clear, cloudy, or opaque.

  • Flocculent Material

    Visible clumps or particles in urine, indicating the presence of cells, crystals, or other abnormal components.

modules.content:
Urinalysis · Instructional module 7 of 10

Urinalysis

Dipstick testing, sediment analysis, and specific gravity, in the document's own words.

0 of 3 sections open

Urine dipstick tests are used to analyze various components of urine, including blood, protein, glucose, pH, and more. The test strip is briefly dipped into a urine sample, ensuring all pads are adequately covered. Excess urine is dabbed off the strip. The strip can be read manually using a color chart or using an automated urine analyzer. If reading manually, results are read after one minute, comparing the color of the pads to the chart. Each pad on the strip corresponds to a specific analyte, and the color intensity indicates the concentration.

Urine sediment analysis involves examining the solid components of urine under a microscope to detect cells, crystals, casts, and other elements. Traditional urine sediment analysis involves preparing slides (wet mounts, stained or unstained, or dry mounts) and examining them under a microscope. Machines can automate the process, analyzing a urine sample and providing results for various sediment components.

A measured pipette and pipette tips specific to the analyzer are used to collect a precise amount of urine. The collected sample is placed in the test well window of the analyzer, and the start button is pressed. The SediView provides results for various sediment components (white blood cells, red blood cells, bacteria, casts, crystals) and may include images to help with interpretation. The veterinary technician visually identifies and quantifies different elements present in the urine sediment under the microscope.

Urine specific gravity measures the concentration of dissolved substances in urine, providing information about kidney function. A refractometer is used to determine the urine specific gravity. A drop of urine is placed on the refractometer slide, the lid is closed, and the reading is taken by looking through the eyepiece. While some urine dipstick tests include a specific gravity measurement, it is not accurate for cats and dogs, making the use of a refractometer essential in veterinary medicine.

modules.content:
Additional Tests & Tips · Section 4 of 4

Additional Tests & Tips

The document's final section. Twelve key terms across fecal analysis, SNAP tests, ear cytology and therapeutic drug monitoring.

Before we get started, let's review a few key terms we'll go over in this upcoming section…

0 of 12 key terms revealed

  • Fecal Flotation

    A diagnostic technique to detect parasite eggs in fecal samples using a solution like Fecasol.

  • Meniscus

    The curved upper surface of a liquid. Ensuring a proper meniscus helps collect floating parasite eggs.

  • Ova

    The term for parasite eggs, typically observed during microscopic examination of fecal samples.

  • Fecal Cytology

    Microscopic analysis of cells in a fecal sample, providing information about bacteria, white blood cells, and pathogens.

  • Motility

    Refers to the ability of an organism to move independently, observed in fecal samples to detect live parasites.

  • Conjugate

    A component in diagnostic tests that binds to the target substance, important for the accuracy of tests like the heartworm 4DX.

  • Control Dot

    An internal control on SNAP tests indicating the test is working properly, even if the result is negative.

  • Ear Cytology

    Microscopic examination of ear canal samples to identify bacteria, yeast, inflammatory cells, and other abnormalities.

  • Oil Immersion Lens

    A high-magnification microscope lens requiring immersion oil, used for detailed observation of samples like ear cytology.

  • Clean vs. Dirty Stain

    Separate stains for different sample types to prevent cross-contamination; 'clean' for blood smears, 'dirty' for ear and fecal cytologies.

  • Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

    Measuring medication levels in blood to ensure safe and effective dosing, for drugs like thyroid medication and phenobarbital.

  • Serum Separator Tubes

    Blood collection tubes with gel to separate blood cells from serum during centrifugation, used in therapeutic drug monitoring.

modules.content:
Additional Tests & Tips · Instructional module 8 of 10

Fecal Analysis

Flotation, cytology and wet mounts, in the document's own words.

0 of 3 sections open

Fecal flotation is a technique used to detect parasite eggs (ova) in fecal samples. The fecal sample is mixed with a solution (e.g., Fecasol) that causes parasite eggs to float to the surface. The mixture is centrifuged to further concentrate the eggs. Additional solution is added to create a meniscus, and a coverslip is placed on top. The sample is allowed to sit for a designated time (e.g., 5 minutes) to allow the eggs to float to the coverslip.

The coverslip is carefully removed and placed on a slide for microscopic examination. The sample is examined systematically under a microscope at 10x magnification to look for parasite eggs.

Fecal cytology is used to evaluate the cellular components of feces, including bacteria, white blood cells, and other cells. A small amount of feces is collected using a wooden applicator stick. The sample is rolled onto a slide with a frosted edge, creating a thin, even smear. The smear is allowed to air dry. The slide is stained using a Diff-Quik stain. The stained slide is examined under a microscope to assess the bacterial flora, look for signs of inflammation (white blood cells), and identify any other abnormal cells.

A fecal wet mount is used to assess for motility, which can help identify certain live parasites. A small amount of feces is placed on a slide. A drop of distilled water is added and mixed with the feces. The sample can be covered with a coverslip or examined directly without one. The wet mount is examined under a microscope at 10x magnification, looking for any signs of movement, which could indicate the presence of live parasites.

Put the steps in order

Put the fecal flotation steps in the document's order

Select each step in the order the document describes it.

0 of 6 steps in order

    Sequence complete. Mix with flotation solution, centrifuge, create the meniscus, add the coverslip, wait the designated time, then transfer to a slide and scan at 10x.

modules.content:
Additional Tests & Tips · Instructional module 9 of 10

Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

Why timing and sample type decide whether a drug level means anything.

0 of 2 sections open

Therapeutic drug monitoring involves measuring the levels of certain medications in the blood to ensure they are within the therapeutic range and adjust dosages if needed.

The timing of blood collection is crucial for accurate results as drug levels fluctuate over time. Some tests require samples to be taken at specific intervals after medication administration. Additionally, certain anticoagulants can interfere with some drug assays, so it's essential to use the correct sample type specified by the lab.

Some therapeutic drug monitoring tests may involve collecting multiple blood samples throughout the day or administering an injection in the hospital and then taking blood samples at pre-determined time points.

What the document says to confirm before you collect

  • The interval after medication administration the ordered test requires.
  • The sample type specified by the lab, because certain anticoagulants can interfere with some drug assays.
  • Whether the test needs multiple samples across the day or timed points after an in-hospital injection.
Knowledge reinforcement

modules.content:
Additional Tests & Tips · Instructional module 10 of 10

Ear Cytology

The last of the document's ten modules: slide setup, the dirty stain rule, staining, and reading.

0 of 3 sections open

Ear cytology is performed to examine the cells present in ear discharge or debris to diagnose ear infections and identify the type of organisms involved (bacteria, yeast, etc.). Samples from the left and right ears are placed on separate areas of the slide, typically near the frosted edge.

It's important to use a "dirty stain" specifically designated for ear cytologies to prevent cross-contamination with clean stains used for other types of samples.

The slide is stained using a Diff-Quik stain, involving a three-step process (fixative, pink stain, purple stain) with 10-15 seconds in each solution as you dip repeatedly. Excess stain is blotted between steps, and the slide is rinsed after staining.

The slide is initially examined at 10x magnification to assess the overall sample quality and staining. Further evaluation is done at 40x magnification. The most detailed assessment is performed using the 100x oil immersion lens to identify bacteria, yeast, white blood cells, and other cells.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of using a purple top tube with EDTA for hematology analysis?
opts: To prevent the blood from clotting
To separate the blood into its components
To stain the blood cells for better visibility
To increase the accuracy of the analyzer
quiz.exp: EDTA is an anticoagulant added to blood collection tubes to prevent clotting, and purple top tubes typically contain EDTA. The document specifies whole blood collected in a purple top tube containing EDTA for hematology analysis.

quiz.q: When preparing a blood smear, what is the importance of the feathered edge?
opts: It allows for easy application of the stain
It indicates if the sample was mixed properly.
It provides an area where cells are spread out in a single layer for optimal viewing.
It helps to determine the total protein concentration.
quiz.exp: The goal of spreading the drop is a feathered edge: a thin area where cells are spread out in a single layer (monolayer), making them easier to view under a microscope.

quiz.q: When preparing a blood sample for analysis using the Catalyst machine, it's acceptable to use any pipette as long as the correct volume of blood is dispensed into the sample cup.
quiz.exp: The document describes collecting the precise volume of plasma using a pipette dedicated to the Catalyst machine, along with measured pipette tips specific to the analyzer elsewhere in the course.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements accurately reflects the use of a refractometer in urinalysis, according to the provided sources?
opts: It is used to determine the pH of the urine sample.
It replaces the need for microscopic examination of urine sediment.
It analyzes the color and clarity of the urine sample, providing a numerical value for each characteristic.
It provides a more accurate measurement of urine specific gravity in cats and dogs compared to dipstick tests.
quiz.exp: While some urine dipstick tests include a specific gravity measurement, the document states it is not accurate for cats and dogs, making the use of a refractometer essential in veterinary medicine.

quiz.q: A veterinary technician is preparing to examine a fecal sample under a microscope to check for the presence of parasitic organisms. Which microscopic technique, as described in the sources, would be most appropriate for this purpose?
opts: Fecal cytology using a Diff-Quick stained dry mount slide
Evaluation of a wet mount slide to assess for motility
Examination of a fecal flotation sample using a coverslip
Analysis of a blood smear stained with Diff-Quick to rule out blood parasites
quiz.exp: Fecal flotation is the technique the document describes for detecting parasite eggs (ova): the eggs float to the coverslip, which is then moved to a slide and examined systematically at 10x magnification.
